Co-citation edges, with the same weights as the coupling measures

Source: R/biblio_cocitation.R
biblio_cocitation.Rd

Builds the edges of a co-citation network from a table of direct citations (one row per citing document and cited reference). Two references are co-cited when at least one document cites both of them (Small 1973) . By default the weight is the co-citation angle (Sen and Gan 1983) : the number of documents citing both references, divided by the geometric mean of the numbers of citations received by each of them. With method, the co-citation can also be weighted like the coupling measures (coupling_strength(), coupling_similarity(), coupling_jaccard(), coupling_vladutz()): see the section on the idf weights below.

Usage

biblio_cocitation(
  dt,
  source,
  ref,
  normalized_weight_only = TRUE,
  weight_threshold = 1,
  output_in_character = TRUE,
  method = c("angle", "strength", "similarity", "jaccard", "vladutz")
)

Arguments

dt

A data frame or a data.table of direct citations, one row per link between a citing document and a cited reference. It is not modified.

source

Character scalar. The column of the citing documents: they are the nodes of the coupling network.

ref

Character scalar. The column of the cited references: they are the nodes of the co-citation network.

normalized_weight_only

Logical. If FALSE, the number of documents citing both references is returned in addition to the normalised weight.

weight_threshold

Number. The minimum number of documents that must cite two references together for them to be linked (1 by default).

output_in_character

Logical. If TRUE (default), the identifiers are also returned as character columns from and to, to build a tidygraph graph more easily.

method

The weight: "angle" (default, the co-citation angle), "strength", "similarity", "jaccard" or "vladutz" (see above).

Value

A data.table with one row per pair of references: the identifiers in from and to (if output_in_character = TRUE), the weight and, if normalized_weight_only = FALSE, nb_shared_citations. The original identifiers are kept in Source and Target. Each pair appears once, with Source < Target.

Details

Write \(C(A)\) for the set of documents citing reference \(A\). The weight of the tie between references \(A\) and \(B\) with the default method = "angle" is

$$w_{AB} = \frac{|C(A) \cap C(B)|}{\sqrt{|C(A)| \, |C(B)|}}$$

The numerator is the number of documents citing both references (returned as nb_shared_citations when normalized_weight_only = FALSE). The other methods are those of the coupling functions, applied to the references as nodes: see the documentation of each, replacing "document" by "reference" and "reference" by "citing document".

Computing choices:

  • \(|C(A)|\) is the number of citations received in the whole table, including from documents that cite only one reference;

  • documents citing a single reference cannot co-cite anything and are ignored in the numerator;

  • duplicated rows are counted once, and rows with a missing identifier are dropped with a warning;

  • the table of the user is not modified;

  • if no pair of references is co-cited (or none reaches weight_threshold), a zero-row table is returned with a warning explaining why.

Memory and speed: the pairs are computed with sparse matrices, as in coupling_angle(); a few documents with extremely long bibliographies still create many pairs. Consider removing them first.

Why use it in research

Where bibliographic coupling looks at what documents use, co-citation looks at how the community perceives cited documents: references that are regularly cited together are considered by citing authors as belonging to the same body of work. Co-citation networks are the classic tool to map the intellectual base of a field (schools, paradigms, canonical references) and to identify the key texts of each cluster (Boyack et al. 2005; Boyack and Klavans 2010; Yan and Ding 2012) . Unlike coupling, a co-citation network is not fixed at the date of publication of the cited documents: it depends on later citations, and thus changes as the corpus of citing documents grows. This is a feature if you want to study how the reception of texts evolves, but it must be kept in mind when comparing time windows. A reference that is rarely cited has a very uncertain position, hence the interest of weight_threshold.

Intuition

Imagine that each citing document is a reading list. Two references that appear together on many lists are probably about related things. The weight with method = "angle" asks: among all the lists where one of the two references appears, how often is the other one there too? A reference cited a thousand times appears on many lists by default, so it must be seen with another reference much more often to be considered close to it: that is what the division by the number of citations does.

Weighting the co-citing documents (the idf methods)

The idf measures of the coupling functions give more weight to a rare shared item. In coupling, the shared items are references, and a reference cited by few documents is rare. Co-citation is the mirror image (Rousseau 2010) : the shared items are the citing documents, and a citing document is "rare" when it cites few references. The intuition is again about reading lists: a document that cites only 8 references and puts A and B among them tells much more about the closeness of A and B than a review that cites 300 references and puts A and B among them by completeness. With method = "strength" (and "similarity"), the co-citation of A and B by a document \(d\) is weighted by \(\log(M / L_d)\), with \(M\) the number of references in the table and \(L_d\) the number of references of \(d\). This is a direct transposition of the formulas of coupling_strength() and coupling_similarity() (swapping the two columns of the table): it is not a measure proposed in the literature as such, so compare it with the default on your corpus (compute_couplings() with network = "cocitation").

References

Boyack KW, Klavans R (2010). “Co-Citation Analysis, Bibliographic Coupling, and Direct Citation: Which Citation Approach Represents the Research Front Most Accurately?” Journal of the American Society for Information Science and Technology, 61(12), 2389–2404. doi:10.1002/asi.21419 .

Boyack KW, Klavans R, Börner K (2005). “Mapping the Backbone of Science.” Scientometrics, 64(3), 351–374. doi:10.1007/s11192-005-0255-6 .

Rousseau R (2010). “Bibliographic Coupling and Co-Citation as Dual Notions.” In The Janus Faced Scholar: A Festschrift in Honour of Peter Ingwersen, 167–173. Royal School of Library and Information Science, Copenhagen.

Sen SK, Gan SK (1983). “A Mathematical Extension of the Idea of Bibliographic Coupling and Its Applications.” Annals of library science and documentation, 30(2).

Small H (1973). “Co-Citation in the Scientific Literature: A New Measure of the Relationship between Two Documents.” Journal of the American Society for Information Science, 24(4), 265–269. doi:10.1002/asi.4630240406 .

Yan E, Ding Y (2012). “Scholarly Network Similarities: How Bibliographic Coupling Networks, Citation Networks, Cocitation Networks, Topical Networks, Coauthorship Networks, and Coword Networks Relate to Each Other.” Journal of the American Society for Information Science and Technology, 63(7), 1313–1326. doi:10.1002/asi.22680 .

See also

Other co-citation and co-authorship measures: coauth_network()

Examples

library(biblionetwork)
# Co-citation network of the references of the stagflation corpus,
# keeping the pairs co-cited at least three times
edges <- biblio_cocitation(Ref_stagflation,
                           source = "Citing_ItemID_Ref",
                           ref = "ItemID_Ref",
                           weight_threshold = 3)
head(edges)
#>      from     to    weight Source Target
#>    <char> <char>     <num>  <int>  <int>
#> 1: 181882 214939 0.2121320 181882 214939
#> 2: 181882 364710 0.3162278 181882 364710
#> 3: 181483 364716 0.6123724 181483 364716
#> 4: 181882 364716 0.2371708 181882 364716
#> 5: 214939 364716 0.3354102 214939 364716
#> 6: 364758 364765 1.0000000 364758 364765

# The same pairs, weighted by the specificity of the co-citing documents
head(biblio_cocitation(Ref_stagflation, "Citing_ItemID_Ref", "ItemID_Ref",
                       weight_threshold = 3, method = "strength"))
#>      from     to     weight Source Target
#>    <char> <char>      <num>  <int>  <int>
#> 1: 181882 214939 0.05536295 181882 214939
#> 2: 181882 364710 0.10082702 181882 364710
#> 3: 181483 364716 0.51473013 181483 364716
#> 4: 181882 364716 0.08730949 181882 364716
#> 5: 214939 364716 0.14425521 214939 364716
#> 6: 364758 364765 1.50258125 364758 364765
